meta.title: Who really said "A diplomat is a man who always remembers a woman's birthday but never remembers her age"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Robert Frost. The joke ran as anonymous newspaper filler in 1896, and in 'diplomat' form by 1912. Frost was first credited only in 1939.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A diplomat is a man who always remembers a woman's birthday but never remembers her age'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traced it to an 1896 newspaper filler credited to a German humour magazine. Robert Frost's name was attached only in 1939.

answer.label: Not Robert Frost — an anonymous newspaper joke from 1896
answer.authorDates: Anonymous newspaper filler, in print from May 1896 · credited to Robert Frost only from 1939
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traced the core of the joke to a filler item in a Rochester, New York newspaper on 10 May 1896, where it was credited to the Munich humour weekly Fliegende Blätter, and found the first version using the word ‘diplomat’ in a 1912 anecdote about the actress Lillian Russell. Frost’s name was not attached until a Tennessee newspaper column in November 1939, and no work of his has ever been shown to contain the line.

source.heading: Where the joke actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Democrat and Chronicle, Rochester, New York — 10 May 1896
The Journal and Tribune, Knoxville, Tennessee — 4 February 1912, in an anecdote about Lillian Russell
The Jackson Sun, Jackson, Tennessee — 5 November 1939, signed only “— Frost”

source.excerpt: Miss Lillian Russell, more beautiful than ever, was serving tea at the Professional Woman’s League bazaar at the Waldorf-Astoria. A member of the Spanish legation passed with two charming girls, and Miss Russell said. “No wonder that young man is so popular with the ladies. He is a ladies’ diplomat.” “How a ladies’ diplomat?” a composer asked. “Well,” explained Miss Russell, “he is the sort of chap who always remembers a woman’s birthday and forgets her age.”
trail: May 1896 — the core joke runs as filler in a Rochester, New York newspaper, credited to the Munich humour weekly Fliegende Blätter: “my wife always wants me to remember her birthday, but to forget her age.” No diplomat, and no author — Quote Investigator ↗

February 1912 — the word ‘diplomat’ appears for the first time, in a syndicated anecdote in which the actress Lillian Russell describes a young man at a Waldorf-Astoria bazaar as “the sort of chap who always remembers a woman’s birthday and forgets her age” — Quote Investigator ↗

1913–1935 — it hardens into a stock definition and circulates as filler for two decades, in trade papers, school journals and newspapers from Springfield to Denver, and finally in John Garland Pollard’s 1935 A Connotary: “Diplomat — A man who remembers a woman’s birthday and forgets her age” — Barry Popik ↗

1939, then 1949 — a Jackson, Tennessee column signs the line “— Frost”, and ten years later Evan Esar’s Dictionary of Humorous Quotations files it under Robert Frost. From there it is a fact in print — Quote Investigator ↗
source.cutTag: The Journal and Tribune, Knoxville, 4 February 1912
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest ‘diplomat’ version Quote Investigator located — an anecdote rather than the modern epigram, and one in which Lillian Russell is repeating a quip that had already been in American papers for sixteen years. The sentence reaches its familiar wording in the 1940s, by which time Frost’s name was already travelling with it.

source.rightsNote: This is an anonymous joke rather than a passage from an identifiable work, so there is no publication date that settles its copyright. The 1890s and 1910s American newspaper printings that Quote Investigator and Barry Popik document are themselves long out of copyright, but the sentence has no known author — so Quotle.info asserts no rights status for the line, and none for the Frost estate, which has no documented claim to it.

author.name: Robert Frost
author.kicker: The name it got pinned to
author.heading: Why Robert Frost?
author.metaLine: 1874–1963 · American poet, four-time Pulitzer Prize winner — and the wrong name on this joke
author.bio: Robert Frost was born in San Francisco in 1874 and became the most publicly celebrated American poet of his century, winning four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry and reading at John F. Kennedy’s inauguration. His first collection, A Boy’s Will, appeared in London in 1913 — seventeen years after this joke had already been running in American newspapers. He was a poet of rural New England, not a writer of newspaper gags, and he has no documented connection to this line beyond a signature an anonymous columnist added to it in 1939.

copyAttribution: "A diplomat is a man who always remembers a woman's birthday but never remembers her age." — not Robert Frost. This is an anonymous newspaper joke: the core appeared in a Rochester, New York paper on 10 May 1896, credited to the Munich humour magazine Fliegende Blätter, and the 'diplomat' version was in print by February 1912 in an anecdote about Lillian Russell. Frost's name was first attached in a Jackson, Tennessee newspaper column on 5 November 1939, and fixed in place by Evan Esar's Dictionary of Humorous Quotations in 1949. Citation trail: Quote Investigator and Barry Popik. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: How Frost got the credit
misattribution.intro: Robert Frost is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for unsourced wit, and this joke is a textbook case. It had been in print for forty-three years before anyone thought of him, and it stuck because a quotation dictionary put it there.

items.why: The earliest Frost credit Quote Investigator located is a column called ‘Wise Sayings Of Wise Men’ in a Jackson, Tennessee newspaper, which printed “A diplomatist is a man who always remembers a woman’s birthday, but never remembers her age” and signed it simply “— Frost”. No work, no date, no context — QI notes only that Robert Frost was probably who was meant — Quote Investigator ↗

items.scope: Evan Esar, The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations (1949), p. 79
items.why: Esar’s dictionary filed the modern wording under “FROST, Robert, born 1875, American poet” — a birth year that is itself wrong, since Frost was born in 1874; Quote Investigator verified that entry from scans — Quote Investigator ↗. The error travelled with the quote: forty years later The Concise Columbia Dictionary of Quotations (1989) still printed “Robert Frost (1875-1963)” beside it — Barry Popik ↗

items.scope: Saturday Review (1959) and The Book of Quotes (1979)
items.why: Once a dictionary carries a line, it simply recirculates. Quote Investigator finds it as the answer to a Saturday Review cryptogram puzzle on 7 November 1959, signed “— ROBERT FROST”, and again in Barbara Rowes’s The Book of Quotes in 1979 — Quote Investigator ↗

The line is still served under Frost’s name with no source at all. Goodreads carries it directly beneath the site’s own notice that “Quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads” — Goodreads ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody has produced a Frost text that contains this joke. It was anonymous newspaper filler in 1896, credited then to a Munich humour magazine, and Frost’s name arrived on it only in 1939 — Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: A joke with a definition’s shape
lead: The line survives because it is built like a dictionary entry, and a definition is the easiest thing in the world to hand to a famous wit. In 1896 it was not about diplomats at all: an American newspaper reprinted a German gag about a husband whose wife wants her birthday remembered and her age forgotten. The same summer two more papers ran their own versions — a sign it was already common property rather than anyone’s property.

The ‘diplomat’ framing arrives sixteen years later, in a 1912 anecdote about Lillian Russell at a Waldorf-Astoria bazaar, and by 1913 it has hardened into the shape everyone now knows: the ‘Pop, what is a diplomat?’ exchange, syndicated from paper to paper with a different city’s newspaper credited each time. Nothing anywhere in that chain has an author. That vacuum is exactly what a famous name eventually fills.
detailsBody: Consider the timing. In May 1896, when the joke first appears in a Rochester newspaper, Robert Frost was twenty-two years old and had published no book. His first collection, A Boy’s Will, would not appear until 1913, in London — the same year the ‘Tommy’s Pop’ version was being syndicated across American papers by writers who had no idea who he was.

Frost went on to win four Pulitzer Prizes for poetry. He was not a gag writer, he had no connection to diplomacy, and no collection of his poems, prose, letters or recorded talks has ever been shown to contain this sentence. Barry Popik, who assembled the citation trail, puts it plainly: there is no evidence Frost either coined or popularised the saying.
context.pull: The line had been in print for forty-three years before anyone thought of Robert Frost.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Robert Frost. The true author is not established; no creator is asserted here. The 1912 printing named in isPartOf carries only the variant wording recorded in alternateName — the modern epigram given here as the quotation text is not attested in that issue, and the saying does not reach its familiar wording until the 1940s.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest located match for the core joke is a filler item in a Rochester, New York newspaper in May 1896, ascribed to the German humour magazine Fliegende Blätter: "my wife always wants me to remember her birthday, but to forget her age." A diplomat was not mentioned in this version.

QI's earliest 'diplomat' version is a 1912 anecdote (Knoxville Journal and Tribune, 4 February 1912, "A Ladies' Diplomat", p. 3A) in which Lillian Russell says a young man "is the sort of chap who always remembers a woman's birthday and forgets her age."

QI's earliest Frost credit is The Jackson Sun (Jackson, Tennessee), 5 November 1939, p. 4, in "Wise Sayings Of Wise Men" by W. A. Caldwell: "A diplomatist is a man who always remembers a woman's birthday, but never remembers her age." — Frost; QI adds "(probably Robert Frost)" and concludes "Robert Frost implausibly received credit by 1939."
Evan Esar's The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations (1949), p. 79, lists the modern wording under "FROST, Robert, born 1875, American poet"; QI notes this citation was verified with scans.
QI records the joke as the answer to a Saturday Review cryptogram on 7 November 1959 signed "— ROBERT FROST", and in Barbara Rowes's The Book of Quotes (1979), p. 279.

Barry Popik states the saying "has often been attributed to American poet Robert Frost (1874-1963) since at least 1949, but there's no evidence that Frost either coined or popularized the saying," and dates it in print to at least 1913.

Popik reprints John Garland Pollard's A Connotary (1935), p. 31: "Diplomat — A man who remembers a woman's birthday and forgets her age", and The Concise Columbia Dictionary of Quotations (1989), p. 79, which credits "Robert Frost (1875-1963) American poet". Popik also reprints 1913 attestations from Implement Age, The School Journal and The Square Deal.
Wikiquote's Robert Frost page does not contain this quote in any section (sourced, attributed, disputed or misattributed), and gives Frost's dates as 26 March 1874 – 29 January 1963.

Robert Frost was born 26 March 1874 and died 29 January 1963; his first collection A Boy's Will was published in 1913 by David Nutt in London; he was the only poet to receive four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry.
The Internet Archive holds Evan Esar's The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations, dated 1949, creator "Esar, Evan, 1899- ed".
Fliegende Blätter was "a German weekly humor and satire magazine appearing between 1845 and 1944 in Munich."

Goodreads displays "A diplomat is a man who always remembers a woman's birthday but never remembers her age." attributed to Robert Frost with no source, beneath the notice "Quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads."
Lillian Russell (born 4 December 1860 or 1861, died 6 June 1922) "became one of the most famous actresses and singers of the late 19th and early 20th centuries."
